title: Forming conscience (CCC 1783–1794)
hookLine: conscience must be educated and can err

cards: A car on a country road at night. The map on the phone hasn't been updated in a long time, and it speaks in the same calm, certain voice it always uses: in a quarter mile, turn left. The driver turns left.
The road is gone: a gate, a field, a sign that says closed. The voice wasn't lying. It was sure.
It was also wrong, because nobody had taught it what changed. The Catechism says an inner voice must be followed, and in the same breath, that it can be wrong.

teach.b: Back on day three hundred ten, you met conscience as the inner sanctuary. Today, how it learns. The Catechism holds two things together.

teach.h: IT CAN ERR, SO IT MUST BE FORMED.
teach.b: First: a person must always obey the certain judgment of their own conscience; acting deliberately against it is wrong. Second: conscience can make mistakes, so it has to be formed, educated, the way a mind is.
It calls this a lifelong task, beginning in childhood. Why? Because people are pulled by bad influences, and tempted to prefer their own judgment and turn from what they're taught.
A well-formed conscience is upright and truthful. Then it names the teachers.

teach.h: THE WORD, THE SPIRIT, OTHERS, THE CHURCH.
teach.b: First, the word of God, taken in through faith and prayer and put into practice: a light for the path, echoing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths."
Alongside it, the gifts of the Spirit, the witness and advice of others, and the Church's authoritative teaching. Then it's honest about error.
Sometimes a person really doesn't know better, through no fault of their own; then the wrong isn't held against them, though it's still a wrong.
But sometimes ignorance is chosen: a person takes little trouble to find out what's true and good, or habit slowly dulls the conscience.

teach.h: THY WORD IS A LAMP TO MY FEET.
teach.b: Then the person shares the blame. So conscience is a voice to obey, and a voice to teach. Both at once.

how: Catholics form their conscience through scripture, prayer, the examination of conscience, advice from others and the Church's moral teaching, and the Church teaches that a certain conscience must always be obeyed.

o: teaching your sense of right and wrong over a lifetime
a feeling of guilt after doing something wrong
following any strong gut feeling without question

s: the Catechism says conscience can never be wrong
it says conscience can err, and so it must be formed.
acting deliberately against a certain conscience is wrong
the Catechism says a person must always obey the certain judgment of conscience.
ignorance that's no one's fault isn't held against them; ignorance from not bothering to find out can be.

games.q: your conscience says one thing firmly. the Church's teaching, and a wise friend, say something else. what does the Catechism ask of you?
o: ignore your conscience and simply comply.
follow conscience, and keep forming it: study, pray, listen.
go with whatever feels right in the moment.
games.why: the Catechism holds both: obey a certain conscience, and keep educating it by the word, prayer, the advice of others and the Church's teaching.

practice: Bring to mind a moral question you have an opinion about but have never really studied, something in the news, at work or at the dinner table, and notice where your view came from: a parent, a feed, a friend, a gut feeling.
Don't change it; just ask what you'd need to read, or who you'd need to hear, to know it better. If you pray, ask for an open mind.

wordCard.voice: Forming conscience. The lifelong work of educating the inner judgment of right and wrong, by the word of God, prayer, the advice of others and the Church's teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: conscience — the word Paul uses for it in his letters.

carryVoice: Your line: an educated conscience. Being sure isn't always the same as being right. Until tomorrow.
